Israel does not celebrate Labor Day on the same date as many other countries. In Israel, Labor Day, also called Yom Ha'avoda, is celebrated on the 1st of Nisan (March/April in the Gregorian calendar) to mark the founding of the national trade union movement of the Histadrut. However, if you are referring to Labor Day that is celebrated on the first Monday in September, which is a common date for many countries, Israel does not celebrate it as a national holiday. Instead, they have Independence Day (Yom Haatzmaut) on the 5th of Iyar (usually in May, based on the Gregorian calendar).

Israel officially canceled Labor Day, known as "Yom Ha'atzmaut," which celebrates the establishment of the State of Israel, and moved the holiday to a different date. Before 1970, Yom Ha'atzmaut was observed on the 5th of Iyar on the Hebrew calendar, which corresponds to early May in the Gregorian calendar.

In 1970, Israel passed the "Holiday and Memorial Day Law," which established Yom Ha'atzmaut as a national holiday to be observed on the 4th of Iyar. The purpose of this change was to move the celebration of the establishment of the state from a date already associated with another Jewish holiday (Yom HaShoah, Holocaust Remembrance Day, which is observed on the 27th of Nissan) to a separate date.

This change aimed to give Israeli citizens a longer and more uninterrupted period to celebrate the anniversary of their country's independence and to honor and reflect on its significance. Since the enactment of this law, Yom Ha'atzmaut is celebrated on the 4th of Iyar each year.
